newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's anti-kidnap chief pans foreign ransoms.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's anti-kidnap chief pans foreign ransoms.

text.p: The head of Colombia's anti-kidnap squad, Alberto Villamizar, condemned multinationals on Tuesday for caving in to ransom demands from leftist guerrillas, but said such payments were not illegal.

The governor of northwestern Antioquia province had angrily accused the German government and German companies on Monday of financing subversion by dealing with the National Liberation Army (ELN) for the release of three kidnapped foreigners.

Two of the three, a Briton and a Dane, were freed over the weekend after a seven-month ordeal. A German seized at the same time was released several months ago, but the German embassy denied on Tuesday it had handed over any ransom.

"Undoubtedly multinational companies harm Colombia by paying these ransoms and giving huge sums to the guerrillas. But although this was once illegal, the constitutional court overturned that law," Villamizar told the Noticiero Nacional TV news.
Earlier he told RCN radio he believed Colombia's guerrillas were using more sophisticated methods to negotiate directly with foreign companies, but did not state exactly what these may be.
Diplomats have said in the past that Colombia's two largest rebel groups are known to operate front companies in several European countries.

Alvaro Uribe, Antioquia governor, sparked a war of words on Monday when he said the German government and German companies had paid $2 million to the ELN for the release of German engineer Karl Heinz Dressel.

Dressel, Briton Philip Halden and Dane Ulrich Shultz had been servicing equipment at cement manufacturer Cementos Rio Claro's new plant in Puerto Triunfo, about 100 miles (160 km) from Medellin, capital of Antioquia, when they were snatched in February.
Dressel worked for the German company Pfister. Halden and Shultz were employed by the Danish concern F.L.Smith, Rio Claro chairman Luis Fernando Ochoa said.
The German embassy issued a terse statement on Tuesday rejecting the governor of Antioquia's statements.

"In accordance with its principles and general practice, the German government does not pay ransoms. As far as the embassy is aware, neither at the moment when the German was freed nor in the release of the other men a few days ago was any ransom paid," it said.
Ochoa said on Tuesday that his company had taken no part in negotiations for the kidnap trio.
